title: Pot-au-Feu
subtitle: French boiled beef and vegetables in broth
excerpt: The national dish of France: a whole piece of beef brisket or shin simmered very gently for hours with vegetables in a clear broth until both the meat and the stock are deeply flavoured. Served as two courses: the broth first, then the meat with its accompaniments.

recipe.sourceNotes: Pot-au-feu (pot on the fire) has been described as the national dish of France since the eighteenth century and as the root from which the whole of French cooking grows: the clear broth produced by simmering meat and vegetables is the base for innumerable French sauces and soups. The dish is served in two stages: the broth (bouillon) is strained and served first, often with small pasta, rice, or vermicelli, or simply with a slice of bone marrow on toast; then the meat and vegetables are served on a platter as the main course, with condiments of coarse salt, cornichons, mustard, and horseradish. The cut of beef is important: a combination of a braising cut (brisket, chuck) with a marrow bone provides the richest broth. The vegetables are added in stages so nothing overcooks: roots go in early, leeks and cabbage late.

content.text: Never let the pot boil; a hard boil makes the broth cloudy and the meat tough. It should simmer so gently that single bubbles occasionally break the surface. Skim the foam thoroughly in the first 15 minutes; a clear broth requires attention at the start. The broth is seasoned at the end, not the beginning, as it concentrates considerably over the long cooking time.

content.text: Put the beef in a large pot and cover with cold water by 6 cm. Bring slowly to the boil, skimming regularly. Once the foam stops rising (about 15 minutes), reduce to the gentlest simmer. Add the onion halves, thyme, bay leaves, peppercorns, garlic, carrot, and celery. Cook uncovered at a gentle simmer for 2 hours 30 minutes.

Add the potatoes and cook for 25 minutes. Add the leeks and cook for 10 minutes. Add the cabbage wedges and cook for 20 minutes. Test the beef: it should be completely tender, yielding easily to a skewer. Season the broth with salt.
Lift out the meat and vegetables. Strain the broth through a fine sieve. Serve the broth first in bowls, then the sliced meat and vegetables on a platter with mustard, coarse salt, and cornichons.
